phonemes.desc: Labiovelar onset [ɡw], as in Welsh Gwyn or English 'Gwen' — a single rounded g, never two separate sounds.
Short open [a] followed by [lx]: the Welsh voiceless velar fricative ch, the rasp of Scottish 'loch', closing the first syllable.
The word Mai, 'May', as a closing diphthong [mai] — the name's second element, 'hawk of May', sounded like the English month.

pronunciation.approximation: GWALH-my — the gw of 'Guinevere', the ch of Scottish 'loch', and 'my' like the month of May. The later English form Gawain runs 'guh-WAYN', stress on the second syllable.

pronunciation.note: Gwalchmai is a transparent Welsh compound: gwalch ('hawk') + Mai ('May'), whence the standard scholarly rendering 'hawk of May' (Bromwich, Trioedd Ynys Prydein; Koch); the PuniCodex lexicon keeps the traditional English gloss 'little falcon' for the same root-image. The temple form Gawain is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the English name is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input.

domains.title: The Courteous Knight
domains.subtitle: The Hawk of May, the Quest Completed, and the Girdle of the Green Chapel
domains.lead: Gawain — Welsh Gwalchmai, Arthur's nephew — is the courteous knight of the Welsh and continental cycles: the one who never came home without the quest he went to seek, the measure against whom Chrétien ranks every other knight of the Round Table, and the man the Green Knight chose to test, at the turning of a year, for the one virtue the pentangle guards — truth.

cards.name: The Hawk of May
cards.desc: Gwalch + Mai: the name itself is a raptor and a season — the spring hawk of the Welsh court.

cards.name: The Pentangle
cards.desc: The five-pointed star Solomon set on Gawain's shield in the Green Knight poem — five fives, and truth at the center of them all.

cards.name: The Green Girdle
cards.desc: The lace of silk and gold kept back from the exchange — worn home as the 'token of untruth' the court turned into a badge of honor.

cards.name: Gringolet
cards.desc: Gawain's horse from Chrétien onward — the mount that carries him, in the Green Knight poem, through the winter forest to the Green Chapel.

symbols.name: The hawk
symbols.meaning: The name made image: gwalch, the raptor of the Welsh genealogies — swift sight, swift return

symbols.name: The pentangle
symbols.meaning: The endless knot of five fives: senses, fingers, wounds, joys, and the five knightly virtues bound by truth

symbols.name: The green girdle
symbols.meaning: The kept-back token: one small failure of truth worn openly, until shame becomes the court's badge

symbols.name: The waxing strength
symbols.meaning: The romancers give him a power that rises with the sun to noon and fails after — the trace the scholars read as a faded solar hero

symbols.name: The nick in the neck
symbols.meaning: The single cut of the third stroke: the wound that is also a judgment, and a verdict he refuses to forget

mythology.lead: Gawain's dossier runs from a Welsh triad to a fourteenth-century masterpiece: in every century someone is testing him, and the test is always the same — not whether he can fight, but whether he will keep faith.

myths.title: The Knight Who Finished the Quest
myths.text: The oldest Arthurian tale in Welsh names him in its great muster at Arthur's court: Gwalchmei mab Gwyar — Gwalchmai son of Gwyar — 'because he never returned home without achieving the quest he had gone to seek; he was the best of walkers and the best of riders; he was nephew to Arthur, the son of his sister, and his first cousin.' In a catalogue of hundreds of warriors, giants, and wonders, that is the whole of his entry, and it is the whole of his character: the Welsh tradition remembers him not for a single exploit but for completion itself — the errand that always comes home.

myths.title: One of the Three Well-Endowed Men
myths.text: The Welsh Triads — the medieval memory-system that files the Island of Britain's heroes in threes — name Gwalchmai son of Gwyar among the Three Well-Endowed Men of the Island of Britain, beside Llacheu son of Arthur and Rhiwallawn Broom-Hair (Triad 4). Rachel Bromwich's edition of the Triads is also the standard witness for his name: Gwalchmai, gwalch 'hawk' + Mai 'May', the 'hawk of May' — a name that stands in Welsh before any French romance ever sang of Gauvain.

myths.title: The Nephew of the King
myths.text: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia (c. 1136) made him Latin and sent him across Europe: Walganus, son of Loth of Lodonesia and Arthur's sister Anna, given as a boy to the service of Pope Sulpicius in Rome, recalled to Britain to be knighted, and made the steel edge of Arthur's Roman campaign — the knight who cuts through the emperor's host and slays the nephew of Lucius. When Mordred's treason calls the army home, Walganus falls at the landing, in the first fighting on the shore, and is buried as the chronicle says. A generation earlier, William of Malmesbury had already written him down as Walwen — and reported his tomb, found at Rhos in Pembrokeshire, fourteen feet long.

myths.title: The Measure of Courtesy
myths.text: In the romances of Chrétien (c. 1160–1190), Gauvain is not the hero of any single quest but the standard against which all the heroes are measured: Erec et Enide ranks him first of the knights of the Round Table, and through Cligés, Lancelot, Yvain, and the Conte du Graal he moves as the court's fixed point — courteous without effort, brave without boasting, the knight whose speech is as ready as his sword. Chrétien lets Perceval's innocence test him and the world test them both; the Continuators of the Perceval give him stranger gifts — a strength that doubles as the sun climbs to noon and fails as it falls — the trace that later scholarship would read as the memory of a solar hero.

myths.tag: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
myths.title: The Bargain of the Green Chapel
myths.text:
At Camelot's New Year feast a giant all in green rides into the hall and offers a Christmas game: any knight may take one stroke at his neck with the great axe, on condition of receiving one in return, a year and a day hence, at the Green Chapel. Gawain takes the challenge and strikes the head clean off; the Green Knight picks it up, reminds him of the tryst, and rides out holding it. The year turns, and Gawain rides north through winter to keep his side of the bargain.

At Hautdesert the lord Bertilak proposes an exchange: each evening they will swap whatever the day has won them. Three days the lord hunts; three days his lady tests Gawain's courtesy in his chamber; and each evening Gawain faithfully renders the kisses he has received — but on the third day he keeps back the green girdle the lady says will preserve his life. At the Green Chapel the axe falls three times: twice withheld, and once, for the kept-back girdle, a nick in the neck. The Green Knight reveals himself as Bertilak, sent by Morgan le Fay; the girdle was the whole point. Gawain wears it home as his 'token of untruth' — and Camelot laughs, and binds a green lace on every shoulder in his honor.

myths.title: The Last Letter
myths.text: Malory's Sir Gawaine is the courteous knight grown tragic: head of the Orkney clan, Arthur's dearest nephew, whose feud with Lancelot — after Gareth and Gaheris are slain in the fire of Guenevere's rescue — drags the fellowship to ruin. Wounded at Dover by Lancelot in the last single combat, he dies of the reopened wound, writing with his own hand the letter that calls Lancelot 'flower of all noble knights' and begs him to come see his tomb. And on the eve of Salisbury Plain he returns in Arthur's dream with a troop of ladies, warning the king not to fight Mordred on the morrow — the nephew still trying, from beyond death, to bring his uncle's last errand home.

lore.syncretism: Gawain's deepest comparative file is Irish. The beheading game itself has its classic Celtic witness in Fled Bricrenn, Bricriu's Feast, where the giant Uath — 'Horror' — offers the Ulster heroes exactly the Green Knight's bargain: strike off my head today, and I strike yours tomorrow. Only Cúchulainn takes the axe twice and kneels for the return stroke; the giant brings the blade down blunt, and the champion's portion is judged his. Kittredge's Study of Gawain and the Green Knight (1916) made the Irish episode the standing source-analogue of the English poem, and the comparison has been refined, never abandoned. The loathly-lady strand of Gawain's story — Dame Ragnelle, whose riddle is answered with sovereignty — has its own Irish kin in the sovereignty-goddess tales, where a hag by a well becomes a queen when a king will kiss her. Within the pantheon his standing kin are [[kai|Cei]] and [[bedwyr|Bedwyr]], the two companions Culhwch pairs beside him, and [[cuchulainn|Cúchulainn]], the only other hero in Celtic story who knelt under the return stroke. The Welsh tradition itself never made him a god; it made him something rarer — the knight every other knight is measured against.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gawain is the Arthurian figure with the longest continuous critical life. Chrétien made him the definition of cortoisie; the Gawain-poet made him the test-case of truth; Malory made him the tragedy of loyalty. Tennyson split him in two, taking his courtesy for the early idylls and his Orkney darkness for the last; the twentieth century gave him back to the scholars — Weston and Loomis argued his solar and Celtic pedigrees, and the Tolkien–Gordon edition of 1925 made Sir Gawain and the Green Knight a fixed star of the English canon. Harrison Birtwistle's opera Gawain (1991) set the Green Chapel to music, and the twenty-first century has filmed the poem twice. Through it all the Welsh name never went anywhere: Gwalchmai still stands in the Triads, the hawk of May, waiting at Arthur's court for the quest to be finished.
lore.extendedMeditation: Gawain is the patron of the errand that must be finished and the word that must be kept — and the Green Knight poem's genius is to show that these are not the same virtue. He finishes everything: the quest, the journey north, the appointment no one would blame him for missing. And still he fails, once, by the width of a green lace — not from cowardice, says the poem, but from love of his own life. The court's answer is the tradition's answer: the failure is not hidden but worn, and what one man wears as his shame the fellowship takes up as its badge. The pentangle on his shield has truth at its center because truth is the one knot that cannot be slipped; everything else — courage, courtesy, purity, fellowship, pity — hangs from it. Gawain asks the question every promise asks: not whether you are brave enough to keep it, but whether you are honest enough to say what it cost.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is transmitted in the Latin alphabet throughout: Middle Welsh writes Gwalchmei in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, Geoffrey of Monmouth writes Walganus, and the Cotton Nero manuscript writes Gawayn. The name's single epigraphic witness is the carved label GALVAGIN(VS) on the Modena Archivolt (c. 1120–1140) — the earliest Arthurian image in art. There is no non-Latin original script to restore, and the canonical English form Gawain is plain ASCII: because the name needs no diacritic, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way — gawain.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release. No form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Gawain is a textual figure with one famous epigraphic witness. The Modena Archivolt — the carved portal relief of Modena Cathedral, dated c. 1120–1140 — depicts an Arthurian rescue scene with the figures labeled in stone: Artus de Bretania, Che (Cei), and GALVAGIN(VS), Gawain himself — the earliest Arthurian image in medieval art, carved a generation before Geoffrey of Monmouth finished the Historia. William of Malmesbury (c. 1125) adds the tradition's one grave: the tomb of Walwen, he reports, was found in his own time on the seashore at Rhos in Pembrokeshire, fourteen feet long. His manuscript witnesses are exact: Culhwch ac Olwen survives in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410); Sir Gawain and the Green Knight survives uniquely in British Library MS Cotton Nero A.x (c. 1400), the small quarto it shares with Pearl, Cleanness, and Patience.
